From assessment to tax bill

Wisconsin property tax begins with a local assessor, ends with a bill from your town, village or city treasurer, and has a fixed appeal path in between. State law sets the steps, so the dates below hold in every county, though your municipality may add details.

The municipal assessor finds, lists and values property. Land is classified by use, in eight classes. A house on untilled land is class 1 residential, and so is an apartment building of up to three units. Values are set as of January 1, so a remodel half finished on that date is assessed as it stood then. The assessor reviews every sale, and the best evidence of market value is a recent arm's-length sale that fits with sales of comparable homes.

Any change to a parcel's total assessment must be reported to the owner in writing under sec. 70.365, at least 15 days before the Board of Review meets, or 30 days in a revaluation year.

Many bodies set a levy, but the town, village or city prepares the bill and collects the first payment for the school district, technical college, county and state. The tax rate is the total levy divided by the municipality's total assessed value. Because the rate is local, two Wisconsin homes with the same assessment can carry different bills.

How to challenge your assessment

Two stages are open to you: the annual Open Book period, then the municipal Board of Review. Start with the assessor.

Open Book is a window when the finished roll can be examined. The assessor must be available for at least two hours, in person, by phone or by video. The clerk posts or publishes the dates at least 15 days ahead, or 30 days in a revaluation year. The Board of Review meets during the 45-day period that begins on the fourth Monday in April, and no sooner than seven days after Open Book.

A formal objection follows strict rules, and missing one can cost you the hearing.

  • Give the Board clerk written or oral notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first scheduled meeting.
  • File the signed Objection Form for Real Property Assessment (PA-115A) before the meeting or in its first two hours.
  • Object to the total value. On an improved parcel you cannot object to only the land or only the building.
  • Put your own estimate of land value and improvement value in writing, with the information behind it.
  • Bring evidence. The assessor's value is presumed correct, and you must show the property is over-assessed compared with sales in the municipality.

The Board may waive the 48-hour notice for good cause, and may accept your filing up to the end of the fifth day of its session if you show extraordinary circumstances. It will not hear a complaint that your taxes are too high. It considers only the assessment or classification of your property.

If the Board of Review keeps your assessment

You have two appeal routes plus a separate money claim. Choose before the deadlines pass, since they run from the date you receive the Board's decision.

Route one is circuit court, by certiorari under sec. 70.47(13). File within 90 days after you receive notice of the decision and pay the filing fee. The court reviews only the written Board record. Route two is an appeal to the Department of Revenue under sec. 70.85, for the current year only and only if you objected to the Board. Revenue must receive your letter within 20 days after delivery of the determination, or within 30 days after the mailing date on the clerk's affidavit. The filing fee is $100, and this route is closed to property assessed above $1 million and to properties in Milwaukee.

The money claim is an excessive assessment claim under sec. 74.37. You must have appealed to the Board of Review first, and you file a signed written claim with the municipal clerk by January 31 of the year the tax is payable. It is unavailable if you already appealed to Revenue or the circuit court, and the tax must be paid on time. If the municipality denies the claim or stays silent for 90 days, you then have 90 days to go to circuit court.

Due dates and deadlines

The dates to remember are the 48-hour notice before the Board of Review, the 90-day court window, the January 31 claim date, and the January 31 and July 31 payment dates.

StepDeadline
Notice of intent to objectAt least 48 hours before the first Board of Review meeting
Written objection (PA-115A)Before or in the first two hours of the first meeting
Appeal to Department of Revenue20 days after delivery, or 30 days after the mailing date on the clerk's affidavit
Certiorari in circuit court90 days after you receive the Board notice
Excessive assessment claimJanuary 31 of the year the tax is payable
Tax paymentsJanuary 31 and July 31, unless the municipality sets another schedule

Bills for the 2026 tax year go out no later than the third Monday in December, which is December 21, 2026. The bill carries the tax for that same year, and full payment or the first installment is due by January 31, 2027. Pay in installments and the second is due July 31.

Missing a payment

If the first installment is not received within five working days after January 31, the whole remaining tax becomes delinquent as of February 1.

Interest on the unpaid portion runs from February 1 at 1% per month, and some counties add a further 1.5% per month. A star in a box on the bill means prior-year taxes are unpaid, and the owner should call the county treasurer about those.

Taxes left unpaid for long enough can cost you the property. After a tax certificate is issued, the county treasurer may file a list of parcels for foreclosure in rem in circuit court under sec. 75.521. The ordinary wait is two years from the date of the tax certificate. It is one year where a city or village has added razing and site restoration costs to the tax, or where the certificate is held by a county with 750,000 or more people or a city that proceeds under sec. 74.87. A county must adopt an ordinance to use this procedure, so ask your county treasurer which process applies to your parcel and how much is owed.

Tax credits and relief programs

Relief for Wisconsin owners comes through credits and programs run by different agencies.

  • First dollar credit: paid on a parcel with an improvement owned by the landowner, and shown on the bill as a reduction of the tax due.
  • Lottery and gaming credit: listed on the bill as a reduction of the net property tax.
  • Homestead credit: an income-based credit for homeowners and renters, paid directly. Call the Department of Revenue Homestead Credit Unit at (608) 266-8641.
  • Property tax deferral loan: for qualifying elderly homeowners through WHEDA at (800) 755-7835. It is repaid when you transfer ownership or move, and the loan becomes a lien on the property.
  • Credit for former service members and surviving spouses: run by the state's department for that group. Wisconsin offers no property tax exemption on the basis of military service.

Property tax when you sell

Account for every unpaid installment before closing, and make sure the new owner is entered on the municipal tax roll. Ask the title company or closing agent how the year's tax will be split between seller and buyer, and ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure on any delinquent amount.

The assessor reviews each sale to decide if it is an arm's-length sale usable for assessments, and that review may include an interior inspection with notice to the owner. After a purchase, the buyer should contact the municipality if no bill arrives, because not receiving a bill does not cancel the duty or the interest. A seller who gets a bill after the sale should give the municipality the new owner's name and address.

When back taxes, repairs and a short timeline make a listing hard, a cash sale as-is can skip repairs and showings. Compare written offers by net proceeds and confirm any unpaid tax is paid at closing.

Frequently asked questions

What property tax relief can Wisconsin homeowners get?

Options include the first dollar credit, the lottery and gaming credit, the homestead credit, a WHEDA deferral loan for qualifying elderly owners, and a credit for former service members and surviving spouses.

When is Wisconsin property tax due?

Payment in full or the first installment is due January 31, and the second installment is due July 31 unless your municipality sets another schedule. The bill for the tax year is mailed in December of that same year. A payment more than five working days late makes the remaining tax delinquent.

How do I appeal my Wisconsin property tax assessment?

Talk to the assessor first, go to Open Book, and then object to the municipal Board of Review. Give notice at least 48 hours before the first meeting and file the written PA-115A form in the first two hours. After the Board decides, you can go to circuit court within 90 days or appeal to the Department of Revenue within 20 days of delivery.

Can the Board of Review lower my tax bill if the rate is too high?

No. The Board only decides whether the value or classification of your property is correct. The rate comes from the levies of local governments.

What happens to unpaid Wisconsin property taxes if I sell?

They must be settled with the sale. Ask the county treasurer for the amount owed and ask the closing agent how it will be paid from the proceeds. If taxes stay unpaid for the statutory period after a tax certificate, the county can foreclose the lien in rem under sec. 75.521.

What the Wisconsin homestead exemption does

This exemption is a shield against creditors. It protects up to $75,000 of an owner's interest in the home they live in. Wis. Stat. 815.20 makes a homestead that a resident owner has chosen and occupies exempt from execution, from the lien of every judgment, and from the owner's debts, up to that amount.

The protection has gaps. Mortgages, laborers' liens, mechanics' liens, purchase money liens and taxes still attach to the property. A judgment creditor holding none of those cannot force a sale of equity that sits inside the $75,000 line.

Plenty of Wisconsin owners search for "homestead exemption" hoping for a property tax break. That relief exists under another name and is covered further down. Keep the two apart so you know which applies to your sale.

How much of the home is protected

Each owner is protected up to $75,000, and spouses can each claim that amount on land owned jointly or as marital property.

TopicRule
Exempt amountUp to $75,000 against execution, judgment liens and debts
SpousesEach spouse may claim up to $75,000 on land owned jointly or as marital property
Liens that still attachMortgages, laborers', mechanics' and purchase money liens, and taxes
Land coveredAt least 0.25 acre if available, no more than 40 acres
Sale proceedsProtected up to $75,000 for 2 years while held to buy another homestead
Homestead credit, tax year 2025Household income under $24,680, maximum credit $1,168

The 0.25 acre and 40 acre limits come from Wis. Stat. 990.01(14), which treats a homestead as the dwelling plus the land reasonably needed to use it as a home.

Which homes and owners qualify

The dwelling can be a house, condominium, mobile home, manufactured home, house trailer or cooperative unit. Section 990.01(14) names each form.

  • Tenants in common qualify when they live on the land with their co-owners' consent, and so does any estate less than a fee.
  • Court annotations to the statute say a land contract buyer has an interest big enough to support the exemption.
  • The same annotations say rent collected from a rented part of the homestead stays exempt.
  • Occupancy counts. A court of appeals decision noted under the statute holds that an owner who moves out with no plan to return, and no plan to sell and buy a new home, loses the protection.

A temporary move does not break the exemption if the owner means to come back. The statute says so directly, and a court of appeals decision in the annotations adds that the exemption is read broadly in the homeowner's favor.

Selling a home that has the exemption

The exemption follows the money. It extends to sale proceeds up to $75,000 for 2 years, provided you hold the funds intending to buy another homestead.

That window helps an owner who is behind on debts and wants out quickly. A decision cited in the annotations holds that owners who permanently leave a home that is for sale, planning to put the proceeds toward a new one, keep the exemption in those proceeds. Park the money in an account that is easy to trace, and talk to a Wisconsin attorney before moving it.

Equity also shapes how clean the title is. The annotations report a Wisconsin Supreme Court holding that when a debtor's equity is under the exempt amount, the home is fully exempt and a docketed judgment has nothing to attach to, so the seller can deliver clear title. With more equity, a judgment lien can reach the portion above the line. If a creditor refuses to release a lien on a home worth less than $75,000, s. 815.20(2) lets the owner ask a court for declaratory relief once the creditor has ignored a demand for a recordable release for 10 days.

Does a spouse have to sign the deed?

Usually, yes. Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(f) requires each spouse to sign a conveyance of a married person's homestead interest, or to join in by a separate conveyance. Transfers between spouses are the exception.

A purchase money mortgage on the property needs only the purchaser's signature. The rule applies even if one spouse alone is on the title. When a spouse is separated or hard to reach, sort that out well before the closing date.

Property tax relief is a different thing

The exemption shields equity from creditors. Property tax relief comes as credits, chiefly the homestead credit and the lottery and gaming credit.

The homestead credit helps lower-income people who own or rent a home that pays Wisconsin property tax. For tax year 2025 the main requirements are:

  • You occupied and owned or rented a dwelling subject to Wisconsin property taxes during 2025.
  • You were a Wisconsin resident for all of 2025 and 18 or older on December 31, 2025.
  • Household income was under $24,680, after a $500 deduction for each qualifying dependent.
  • You, or your spouse, had earned income, was disabled, or was 62 or older at the end of 2025.
  • You will not claim the farmland preservation credit or the property tax credit for former service members and surviving spouses in the same year.

The maximum credit is $1,168. Property taxes count when levied for 2025, whenever you pay them. Schedule H-EZ is open only to people who did not sell their home during 2025, so a seller usually files the longer Schedule H. The Department of Revenue's line for questions is (608) 266-2486.

Lottery and gaming credit when you sell

This credit goes with the property, so put it on your list when you prorate taxes at closing. After a sale it stays with a qualifying property and comes off the net tax payable on the next bill.

  • To qualify, you must be a Wisconsin resident who owns the dwelling and uses it as a primary residence on the January 1 certification date.
  • A person can claim only one primary residence. Rental units, vacant land and garages do not qualify.
  • A buyer who is not living there as a primary residence files Form LC-400 with the county treasurer to remove the credit.
  • A buyer who purchased after January 1 can apply if the prior owner used the home as a primary residence on January 1.

If your bill lacks the credit, apply to the municipal treasurer by January 31 after you receive the bill. A late claim goes to the Department of Revenue by October 1.

Checks before you accept a cash offer

Settle three questions before signing: who holds liens, whether every spouse will sign, and where the proceeds will sit. Each ties back to the exemption.

  • Ask the county register of deeds for copies of any recorded judgment, mortgage or lien against the property.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the current tax bill so the credit and the proration come out right.
  • Make sure the contract and deed carry each spouse's signature wherever s. 706.02(1)(f) calls for it.
  • Decide where the sale money will rest during the 2-year proceeds window.

A Wisconsin owner selling as-is must still hand over a condition report on one-to-four unit property within 10 days after the contract is accepted, unless an exemption applies. Raise that early so closing holds no surprises.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Wisconsin homestead exemption?

It is $75,000 per owner. Spouses can each claim up to $75,000 on land they own jointly or as marital property, under Wis. Stat. 815.20(1). Mortgages, mechanics' liens, purchase money liens and taxes sit outside the shield.

Does the exemption protect me if I sell the house?

Yes, for a limited time. Sale proceeds stay exempt up to $75,000 for 2 years while you hold them to buy another homestead. Spending the money on something else can cost you that protection.

Is the homestead credit the same as the exemption?

No. The homestead credit is a lower-income tax credit. For tax year 2025, household income must be under $24,680 and the maximum credit is $1,168. The exemption is creditor protection with no income test.

Does my spouse need to sign if only my name is on the deed?

In most cases yes. Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(f) requires each spouse to sign or join in a conveyance of a married person's homestead interest, except for transfers between spouses. Have the title company review the deed before closing.

What if a creditor has a judgment against me?

The judgment lien cannot attach to equity inside the $75,000 exemption. If your home is worth less than that and the creditor will not release the lien within 10 days after a demand, s. 815.20(2) lets you ask the court for declaratory relief. Confirm details with a Wisconsin attorney.

State tax on a death

Wisconsin dropped its estate tax for anyone who died on or after January 1, 2008. The old inheritance tax return covered only deaths before January 1, 1992. So a family taking over a house from a recent death owes no state tax for the deed passing to them.

An heir who plans to sell can still face other bills. There is the federal estate tax (only for very large estates), income tax on profit from the sale, and a county transfer fee charged when a deed is recorded. Each follows separate rules, taken up next. For a death before those cutoff years, the Department of Revenue can say which return applied.

Federal estate tax

A single house almost never triggers it. A federal return is due only when the gross estate, adding adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, tops the filing threshold for the year of death. The figure is $15,000,000 for 2026, $13,990,000 for 2025 and $13,610,000 for 2024.

Gross estate means everything the person owned or held certain interests in, at fair market value on the date of death. Debts such as a mortgage, costs of administering the estate, and property going to a surviving spouse or a qualified charity are subtracted. Most relatively simple estates have no filing duty.

One more detail: a surviving spouse can choose to carry over the decedent's unused exemption, but only by electing on an estate tax return filed on time. If the estate you are settling comes close to the threshold, hire an estate attorney or tax preparer. A title company will not handle this.

Income tax on the sale

Profit from the sale is taxable, though Wisconsin softens it. Capital asset gains and losses are reported on both the state and federal returns. For assets held longer than one year, the state generally lets you deduct 30% of the net capital gain. The Department of Revenue's Publication 103 is written for 2025 returns.

Gain equals the sale price minus basis. Basis normally means what the owner paid, but inherited property follows separate rules found in IRS Publication 551. Have the estate's tax preparer pin down the basis before you weigh offers, since it sets the tax result.

  • Individual heirs use Wisconsin Schedule WD. Estates and trusts use Schedule 2WD attached to Form 2, Wisconsin Fiduciary Income Tax for Estates and Trusts.
  • On a Wisconsin return, a net capital loss offsets up to $3,000 of other income ($1,500 for married filing separately), starting with tax year 2023. Bigger losses carry forward.
  • State and federal basis sometimes differ. Ask the preparer if an adjustment is needed.

Transfer fee

The rate is 30 cents per $100 of value, and the seller owes it. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) has the register of deeds take payment when the deed is handed in to be recorded, together with a transfer return signed by both parties to the deed.

Inheriting is not selling. When the house moves to heirs by will, descent or survivorship, Wis. Stat. 77.25(11) exempts it. When the estate sells to an outside buyer, no exemption applies and the price is what gets charged.

Transfer typeHow the fee applies
Estate or heirs sell to a buyerFee on the sale price
House goes to heirs by will, descent or survivorshipExempt
One heir pays siblings or the estate to keep the houseFee on the amount paid, exemption for the rest
Trustee deeds to a beneficiary, no paymentExempt
Gift between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, for nominal or no considerationExempt

Returns go in electronically unless a hardship waiver is granted. If a deed claims an exemption, it must name the 77.25 subsection right on its face.

Small estates and the affidavit route

Only small estates qualify. Wis. Stat. 867.03 allows collection by affidavit by certain people (an heir, a revocable trust's trustee, the will's named personal representative, the decedent's guardian) if the Wisconsin property subject to administration is worth no more than $50,000 gross. A house valued above that figure takes the estate out of the affidavit route on its own.

The named personal representative cannot take real estate this way unless also an heir, the trustee of the decedent's own revocable trust, or the guardian. A representative outside those categories waits 30 days after the affidavit is received. Bigger estates need a full probate case. Before a buyer can close, call the circuit court's probate office in the decedent's home county and ask what paperwork it wants.

How an estate sale usually unfolds

Order matters here, because each step feeds the next. Start by finding out whether probate is needed at all, since that decides who can sign. If the estate is small enough for an affidavit, the heir collects the house that way. If not, the court appoints someone with authority, and a buyer will want proof of it before closing.

Next comes the tax picture. The preparer sets the basis, estimates any gain, and tells you whether a federal return is even in question. With that number in hand you can compare a cash offer against a listing without guessing about what you would keep after taxes.

At closing, the seller's side of the statement carries the transfer fee, and the register of deeds takes the transfer return when the deed is recorded. Heirs who are buying out other heirs should raise that with the preparer before the deed is drafted, so the exemption wording is right. Bring the death certificate details, the deed, and any court paperwork that shows who speaks for the estate.

Before you accept a cash offer on an inherited house

Selling for cash is still selling, so the fee and gain rules above stay in play. Run through these before signing:

  • Get the house's basis and a rough gain figure from the estate's tax preparer, plus the schedule that reports it.
  • Ask the register of deeds in the county how the transfer return and exemption number should read on a deed moving title to heirs with no payment.
  • Put in writing who may sign for the estate. Ask the probate office what proof of that authority a buyer will expect.
  • Make sure the closing statement shows the transfer fee as a seller charge.
  • If one heir is buying out the others, tell the preparer. That payment carries the fee.

A cash sale avoids lender appraisals and financing delays. It does not avoid these tasks. Finish them first and closing day goes quickly.

Frequently asked questions

Does Wisconsin have an inheritance tax?

No. The inheritance tax return covered only deaths before January 1, 1992, and Wisconsin has no estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2008. Someone inheriting a house from a recent death owes neither on the transfer.

How large must an estate be before a federal estate tax return is required?

For a 2026 death the threshold is $15,000,000. The gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption is measured against it. Most relatively simple estates never file.

Do heirs pay tax when they sell an inherited house in Wisconsin?

They may owe income tax on the gain, meaning sale price minus basis. Wisconsin generally lets you deduct 30% of net capital gain on assets held over one year. The estate's tax preparer can work out basis and the likely result.

Is the Wisconsin transfer fee due when a house passes under a will?

No, Wis. Stat. 77.25(11) exempts transfers by will, descent or survivorship. The fee of 30 cents per $100 comes into play on a sale, and the price is what it is measured on.

Can a Wisconsin estate use an affidavit instead of probate for a house?

Only if the Wisconsin property subject to administration is worth no more than $50,000 gross. A named personal representative cannot take real estate by affidavit unless also an heir, the trustee of the decedent's revocable trust, or the guardian.

How an eviction case moves through court

Evictions in Wisconsin are heard as small claims cases in the county circuit court, whatever amount of rent is claimed. Chapter 799 of the Wisconsin Statutes sets the procedure, and the court system's small claims self-help pages carry an eviction guide and a forms assistant.

The person entitled to possession, or an agent authorized in writing, files the case under Wis. Stat. 799.40. A claim for money tied to the tenant's occupancy, such as unpaid rent, can ride along, but the complaint has to state it separately. Under 799.41 the complaint is written, names the parties, identifies the property (a street name and number is enough), and lays out the facts that justify removal.

Either side may appear alone or through an attorney. Under 799.06(2), an agent or authorized employee of a company counts as the company appearing in its own person.

Deadlines after filing

Several short clocks run once the case is filed. Your own summons and any court order carry the exact dates, so read them closely.

StepTime limit or rule
Summons return dateSet 5 to 25 days after the summons issues; tenant served at least 5 days before the return date
Judgment and writIf the landlord is entitled to possession, the court enters judgment for restitution and orders a writ issued at once
Hardship stayCourt may stay the writ up to 30 days, on condition that rent and occupancy charges are paid
Emergency assistance stayCase is stayed while the tenant applies, for no more than 10 working days, and not after a writ issues
Sheriff actsExecutes the writ within 10 days of receiving it; a writ received more than 30 days after issuance is not executed
AppealMust start within 15 days of the judgment or order

Can a tenant delay or stop an eviction?

Only in narrow ways. A judge may grant a hardship stay of up to 30 days from the order for judgment, but the stay holds only if the tenant pays all rent and charges due at judgment plus the reasonable value of occupancy during the stay. A bond can be required too. Miss a condition and the landlord files an affidavit, after which the writ can issue immediately.

Filing an appeal does not freeze things by itself. Under Wis. Stat. 799.445 the stay applies only if the tenant files an undertaking with surety the judge approves. That undertaking covers appeal costs plus rent and damages that build up during the appeal. If the tenant then skips rent, the guaranteed payment goes straight to the landlord and the stay ends, freeing the sheriff to execute the writ.

  • A landlord who takes past due rent after notice or after filing cannot be pushed into dismissal on that basis (799.40(1m)).
  • Having waived an earlier lease breach is no defense to eviction or to a damages claim (799.40(1s)).
  • If the tenant is being evicted after a foreclosure sale, the complaint must say so (799.41(2)), and the court stays the case against a foreclosed homeowner as provided in Wis. Stat. 846.40(9) (799.40(4)(b)).

Belongings when the sheriff executes the writ

The sheriff removes the tenant and anyone claiming under the tenant, using reasonable force if needed, then deals with the property under Wis. Stat. 799.45. The landlord picks between two routes. By default the sheriff moves the property to a safe place in the county and mails the tenant written notice of where it is within 3 days. The sheriff may ask the landlord for a deposit toward moving costs first.

The other route is for the landlord to say, when handing over the writ, that the landlord will remove and store or dispose of the property under Wis. Stat. 704.05(5). The sheriff then supervises if asked.

  • Property the sheriff judges worthless can go to a refuse site, with notice to the tenant within 3 days.
  • Prescription medication and prescription medical equipment must be held for 7 days after the landlord finds it, and returned promptly if the tenant asks before disposal.
  • Before disposing of a manufactured home, mobile home or titled vehicle, the landlord must notify the tenant and any secured party the landlord knows about.
  • A landlord who will not store belongings must say so in writing when the lease is signed or renewed.

What to gather before filing

The court will look for proof that the notice was proper and delivered a listed way, so keep the paper trail in one folder. This list follows the statutes, not any local form.

  • The signed lease or rental terms, including any signed term on showing the premises or storing belongings.
  • A rent ledger that separates rent from late fees, because the notice statute counts late fees on past due rent as rent.
  • A copy of the notice and proof of how it was delivered. For certified mail, proof of mailing from the post office is enough under 799.40(1g).
  • The rental's street address, which identifies the property in the complaint.
  • A plan for the tenant's belongings: sheriff storage, or your own removal and storage under 704.05(5).

The county circuit court clerk can tell you which forms and fees apply locally. Ask before you file.

Selling a house with a tenant or a pending eviction

A sale does not wipe out the tenancy. A tenant who is not in default has exclusive possession under Wis. Stat. 704.05(2) until the lease expires or a periodic tenancy is terminated. The landlord may show the premises to buyers on advance notice at reasonable times, unless a signed lease provision says otherwise.

An owner weighing a sale has two paths. One is to finish the notice and court steps above and deliver an empty house. The other is to sell with the tenant staying, which skips the court process. The first path's timeline hinges on the return date the court sets and, after judgment, the sheriff's 10-day window. Those dates vary case by case, so a closing date should come after them, not before.

Buyers who pay cash often accept a house with a tenant or a case in progress, which spares the owner from timing a closing around the sheriff.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an eviction take in Wisconsin?

The statutes set pieces of the timeline rather than one total. The summons return date falls 5 to 25 days after issue, and after judgment the sheriff has 10 days from receiving the writ to execute it. A hardship stay of up to 30 days or an appeal can add time.

Can a Wisconsin tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent?

Late rent paid after notice does not by itself end the case, since a landlord who accepts it cannot be forced to dismiss. A hardship stay of up to 30 days is possible at judgment, and it depends on paying rent and occupancy charges.

How long does a tenant have to appeal a Wisconsin eviction judgment?

Fifteen days from the judgment or order. An appeal pauses enforcement only if the tenant files an undertaking with approved surety covering costs, rent and damages during the appeal.

Who removes a tenant after the court rules for the landlord?

The sheriff. The court orders a writ of restitution, the writ goes to the sheriff, and the sheriff removes the tenant and anyone claiming under the tenant. The sheriff must act within 10 days of receiving it.

Can a Wisconsin landlord ask for back rent in the eviction case?

Yes. Wis. Stat. 799.40(2) lets the landlord join a claim arising from the tenant's possession or occupancy, such as rent owed. The complaint states that claim separately from the request for possession.

What a quitclaim deed does

A quitclaim gives the buyer only what the grantor actually owns, with no pledge that it is much or even anything. Sec. 706.10(4) says it passes all of the interest in or appurtenant to the land that the grantor could lawfully convey, without warranting or implying the existence, quantity or quality of that interest.

Nothing backs up the title, so a title company may balk. Ask early. Compare a warranty deed: sec. 706.10(5) reads into it covenants that the grantor is lawfully seized of the land, can convey it, and that no encumbrance burdens it.

A conveyance is valid once it identifies the parties, land and interest, is signed by each grantor and is delivered. Read the deed closely before signing.

Requirements for a valid deed

A Wisconsin conveyance has to satisfy the formal requisites in sec. 706.02, and a deed headed for recording faces a few formatting rules on top. Check each item below first.

  • It names the parties, the land, and the interest conveyed.
  • Each grantor signs it, or someone signs for the grantor.
  • It is delivered to the grantee.
  • If it gives up a married person's interest in a homestead, each spouse signs or joins in by a separate conveyance. Transfers between spouses are the exception.
  • It carries a form of authentication allowed by sec. 706.06 or ch. 140, and filers are told to bring a notarized deed to the register.
  • It describes the land well enough for the county indexes and, for most documents, includes the full legal description.

Page layout counts too. A register can reject a document that strays from the standard format in sec. 59.43(2m). Leave 0.5 to 6 inches at the top of page one for the document title, and keep a blank 3 inch by 3 inch box in the upper right corner for the recording stamp, with return information also on that page. Use white paper, at least 20 pound, 8.5 inches wide by 11 or 14 inches long, and black, blue or red ink. If your county asks for it, write in the parcel identification number from the tax bill.

Transfer fee and exemptions

No fee is owed only when an exemption fits. Otherwise the grantor pays 30 cents per $100 of value, which is $3 per $1,000, and the register collects it as the deed comes in.

For a sale, value is the full price actually paid, counting liens. A gift, a token-payment deed or a swap is measured by the estimated open market price instead. That means a free quitclaim between relatives still has a market-value basis unless an exemption applies, and the deed has to name the exemption's subsection number on its face.

Type of transferSec. 77.25 subsection
Corrects or confirms a prior recorded deed, for nominal, inadequate or no consideration(3)
Parent and child, stepparent and stepchild, parent and son-in-law or daughter-in-law, grandparent and grandchild, for nominal or no consideration(8)
Between husband and wife(8m)
Between an individual and a domestic partner under ch. 770(8n)
Between agent and principal, or trustee to beneficiary without actual consideration(9)
By will, descent or survivorship(11)
Real estate worth $1,000 or less(13)

The rows above are a sample, so read all of sec. 77.25 for your own situation. If nothing fits, the fee is owed. Checking the value and the exemption is the Department of Revenue's job, not the register's. When it finds value understated by 25% or more, or a wrong exemption, the penalty is the larger of $25 or 25% of the extra fee. Lying about value on purpose can mean a fine up to $1,000, up to one year in county jail, or both.

Recording a quitclaim deed

The sequence is: file a transfer return online, print the receipt, then take the receipt, the notarized deed and payment to the county register of deeds where the land is. Certain counties take the whole package electronically, so look at the county's website.

The return goes through My Tax Account at the Department of Revenue, no login needed. Choose the county and Quit claim deed as the type. Use the signing and delivery date as the conveyance date. Enter each grantor and grantee, spouses separately. With no appraisal on hand, an estimate can be drawn from the latest property tax bill. Only exemption numbers that fit your document and parties will appear.

The $30 recording fee per document is paid up front. Each document is stamped with date, hour and minute and recorded as received. Leave any individual's Social Security number off the deed, since a document containing one cannot be recorded.

List an authorized recipient and include enough postage, and the recorded deed is mailed to that person. A group of related documents sent together can be returned unrecorded if just one breaks the format rules, so send a clean deed. For return questions, write RETR@wisconsin.gov or call (608) 264-6885.

Record promptly. Sec. 706.08 makes an unrecorded conveyance void against a later buyer who acts in good faith, pays value and records first.

What to bring to the register of deeds

Bundle everything before you go or mail it. You will want the signed and notarized deed, the printed transfer return receipt, a check or other payment for the recording fee and any transfer fee, and the name and mailing address of whoever should get the recorded copy. If the county asks for a parcel number, copy it straight from the tax bill so the index entry lines up with the tax roll.

When the deed claims an exemption, double-check that the subsection number on the deed matches the one chosen on the return. A mismatch is the kind of small slip that sends a package back and delays the transfer on the public record.

Using a quitclaim when you sell

Maybe, if the buyer and title company agree. A quitclaim gives no warranty, so learn which deed form they insist on before you sign.

The exemptions in sec. 77.25 point to the usual non-sale uses: transfers within a family, between spouses, and deeds that correct a prior recorded deed.

A house with repair needs, back taxes or an estate history may suit a cash as-is sale instead. Weigh what each offer actually pays at closing, and ask who handles the transfer fee, which falls on the grantor by statute.

Removing a person from the title of a mortgaged home with a quitclaim is a step to clear with the lender and a Wisconsin attorney. A deed giving up a spouse's homestead interest needs both spouses to sign.

A workable order: confirm the form the buyer wants, pull the legal description and parcel number off the tax bill, file the transfer return, notarize the deed, record it, and keep the recorded copy.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed enough to transfer a house in Wisconsin?

Yes, when it satisfies sec. 706.02: parties, land and interest identified, every grantor's signature, and delivery. Recording protects it against later purchasers. No warranty comes with it.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Wisconsin?

The register charges $30 per document. The grantor also owes 30 cents per $100 of value unless sec. 77.25 exempts the transfer. Copies are $2 for page one and $1 for each added page.

Do I need a notary for a Wisconsin quitclaim deed?

Recording requires an authentication form allowed by sec. 706.06 or ch. 140, and notarized deeds are what filers are told to bring. Your county register can confirm any local rule.

Does a spouse have to sign a Wisconsin quitclaim deed?

If the deed gives up a married person's interest in a homestead, each spouse must sign or join by separate conveyance. Conveyances between spouses are the exception under sec. 706.02(1)(f).

Where do I file a Wisconsin quitclaim deed?

At the register of deeds in the county that holds the land. The transfer return goes to the Department of Revenue first, and the receipt goes with the deed.

What is a transfer on death deed in Wisconsin?

It is a recorded document that names who receives a piece of Wisconsin real estate when the owner dies, with no probate case needed for that property. The law behind it is Wis. Stat. 705.15, which describes a "TOD beneficiary designation" made on a recorded document. People call it a transfer on death deed, and the register of deeds treats it as one.

Five kinds of ownership can use it:

  • An interest held by one individual and by no one else
  • A fractional interest held as a tenant in common
  • An interest held by a spouse as marital property
  • An interest held by spouses as survivorship marital property
  • An interest held by two or more people as joint tenants

The transfer happens on the death of the sole owner, or of the last of several owners to die. Until then the beneficiary owns nothing.

What the designation must say

The document has to name the owner or owners, name the beneficiary, and state that the transfer takes effect only on the owner's death. For marital property held by a spouse, both spouses with an interest must sign. Section 705.15(2)(a) lays out these requirements.

The wording is flexible. An owner can write "transfer on death" or "pay on death," or use the letters TOD or POD, placed after the owner's name and ahead of the beneficiary's name. Primary beneficiaries can be listed along with contingent ones, who take if a primary beneficiary does not survive. The designation can go on the original deed that gave the owner title, or on a later document signed and recorded by the sole owner or by all surviving owners.

Capacity matters. The mental capacity needed to sign or cancel a designation is the same as the capacity needed to make or revoke a will under s. 853.01.

Recording is what makes the document work. A designation is ineffective unless the document and the recording fees reach the register of deeds in the county where the land sits before the sole or last owner dies. A signed paper in a drawer does nothing.

Can the owner still sell or change the plan after signing?

Yes. Under section 705.15(3)(a), a designation does not affect ownership until the sole or last owner dies, even if the document says otherwise. The owner keeps full control, and subsection (3)(c) adds that the rule does not limit a transfer made during the owner's life. A sale, a gift or a mortgage during life is still possible.

To cancel or change a designation, the owner records a new instrument. It has to meet every one of these tests:

  • It is a new designation document, an instrument of revocation, or a lifetime deed that expressly revokes the earlier recorded document, in whole or in part
  • The owner acknowledged it after acknowledging the earlier document
  • It reaches the register of deeds in the property's county before the sole or last owner dies

When several owners signed one designation, one owner's revocation does not undo the designation for another owner's interest. For joint tenants or spouses with survivorship marital property, the designation is revoked only if all living joint tenants or spouses revoke it.

What happens to the house when the owner dies

Ownership passes to the surviving beneficiaries, subject to any lien or encumbrance on the property. If a named beneficiary died first, that beneficiary's issue who would take under s. 854.06(3) step in. If nobody qualifies, the interest goes to the deceased owner's estate. Chapter 854 applies to these transfers.

The beneficiary then needs paper proof of title. Section 705.15(5) points to three routes: s. 863.27, s. 865.201 or s. 867.046. The last one runs through the register of deeds. The beneficiary files a signed, sworn application with the decedent's name, residence and address, the applicant's details and the date of death. For real estate the applicant adds the most recent property tax bill, a legal description and a copy of the deed that created the TOD interest. Once recorded, the application ends the decedent's interest with the same force as an order from the probate court of the decedent's home county.

Three timing rules matter:

  • If the beneficiary or personal representative has not started a confirmation within 90 days of death, any interested person may apply under s. 867.046(2m).
  • A claim to recover real property that went to a TOD beneficiary is barred unless a complaint and a lis pendens are filed within 120 days after the death (s. 705.15(8)).
  • A good-faith buyer or lender who deals with the petitioner takes title free of claims by the decedent's estate (s. 867.046(6)).

Recording fees and transfer taxes

Recording costs $30 per document under s. 59.43(2)(ag), and the register may refuse a document that misses its format rules. Those rules include a blank 3-inch by 3-inch space in the upper right corner of page one, the drafter's name, a legal description, no Social Security number, and a parcel identification number in counties that require one.

The state real estate transfer fee does not apply. Under s. 77.25(10m), a conveyance made solely to designate a TOD beneficiary is exempt, and under s. 77.25(11m) so is the nonprobate transfer at death. When removing a decedent's interest, the filer submits a Real Estate Transfer Return in My Tax Account, picks "Termination of Decedent's Interest," and claims exemption 11m if a TOD document was recorded before death. The filer enters the recorded document number and an estimated value taken from the most recent tax bill. Questions go to the Department of Revenue at RETR@wisconsin.gov or (608) 264-6885.

Pay the recording fee of $30 per documentRegister of deedsWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag)
Claim the transfer fee exemptionDocument and transfer returnWis. Stat. 77.25(10m), (11m)
Confirm the beneficiary's interest after deathRegister of deeds applicationWis. Stat. 867.046(2)

Selling the house as a beneficiary

A beneficiary can sell once the interest is confirmed and any liens are dealt with. The property passes subject to liens, so a mortgage or tax debt does not vanish at death. It stays on the title until paid, which makes a payoff figure the first thing to ask a title company for.

A beneficiary who lives far away or inherits a house that needs repairs may want to sell quickly. Line up the confirmation paperwork first: the register of deeds application, the recent tax bill and the recorded designation. A cash buyer can often close without the owner making repairs, but the title still has to be confirmed in your name before closing.

If the estate has an open informal administration, the Wisconsin court system offers form PR-1827, a statement of termination or confirmation of interests in property tied to ss. 705.15, 865.20 and 865.201. An attorney or personal representative completes it, and a certified copy or duplicate original may be recorded with the register of deeds.

A rough path to closing: gather the recorded designation and a death certificate, file the application with the register of deeds, record the confirmation, get a payoff figure for any mortgage or tax debt, and then sign the sale contract. An attorney can say which path suits a particular family.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Wisconsin transfer on death deed avoid probate?

Yes, for the property named in it. Section 705.15 lets the property pass to the designated beneficiary without probate, but only if the designation was recorded with the register of deeds before the last owner died. Other assets without a beneficiary can still need a probate case.

Does the beneficiary have to consent to the designation?

No. The owner signs, and both spouses sign for marital property, but no beneficiary signature is required. The owner can revoke the designation by recording a new instrument without involving the beneficiary.

How much does it cost to record a TOD designation in Wisconsin?

The register of deeds charges $30 per recorded document under s. 59.43(2)(ag). The state transfer fee does not apply because s. 77.25(10m) exempts a conveyance made solely to designate a TOD beneficiary. Call the register of deeds in the property's county about local recording requirements.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

The property goes to the predeceased beneficiary's issue who would take under s. 854.06(3). If no beneficiary or qualifying issue survives all owners, it passes to the estate of the sole or last owner. A contingent beneficiary named in the document takes before that point.

Can the owner still sell the house after naming a beneficiary?

Yes. The designation does not change ownership until death, and s. 705.15(3)(c) leaves lifetime transfers untouched. A sale during life ends the owner's interest, so nothing is left for the designation to pass at death. Ask an attorney before signing a deed.

How Wisconsin probate works

Probate is the court-supervised process that moves a dead person's assets to those entitled to them. Chapters 851 through 882 of the Wisconsin Statutes govern probate actions.

Administration gives notice to creditors and interested persons, identifies heirs and beneficiaries, collects and inventories assets, pays taxes and claims, and then transfers what remains. An informal administration guide revised November 2025 is posted by the courts for people handling an estate themselves.

File in the county where the decedent lived. If the person was not a Wisconsin resident, the application can go to any Wisconsin county where the person owned property.

Which type of probate fits an estate with a house?

The answer depends on the estate's size, whether there is a will, and whether the heirs agree.

Probate pathWhen it applies
Transfer by affidavitProperty subject to administration of $50,000 or less in gross value
Summary settlement$50,000 or less with a surviving spouse, domestic partner or minor children
Summary assignment$50,000 or less, for estates that cannot use summary settlement
Informal administrationSupervised by the Probate Registrar, no continuous court supervision
Formal administrationContinuous court supervision, and an attorney is needed
Register of deeds confirmationSpouse or beneficiary of a marital property agreement or TOD interest

Court staff cannot pick a path for you, since that is a legal decision. Talk to an attorney, especially when heirs disagree, claims are disputed or taxes are an issue.

If the owner died without a will

The estate still goes through administration, and the law decides who the heirs are. Wis. Stat. 852.01 sets out who counts as an heir when there is no will, and a surviving domestic partner is treated like a surviving spouse.

Shares split under the per stirpes rule: property divides at each generation, with one share for each surviving person and one for each deceased person, and a deceased person's share passes to that person's issue. With three children, the children's portion divides into thirds, and if one child has died leaving two children, that third splits between the two grandchildren.

Informal administration of an intestate estate can be denied when the heirs do not all consent in writing or when an interested person demands formal proceedings. Any heir can make that demand, which puts the case in front of a judge.

Selling an inherited house as personal representative

You can sell once the court has appointed you and issued letters. Being named in a will is only a nomination. The Probate Registrar or a judge must appoint you, and the proof is a document called Domiciliary Letters.

  • Sign the deed with the legal description of the land, not the street address. A mistake in the legal description can affect ownership.
  • Deliver the original will and any codicils to the court.
  • Plan to inventory the home at its fair market value on the date of death.

A named personal representative also cannot use the small estate affidavit to take real estate. Wis. Stat. 867.03(1h) bars that unless the person is also an heir, a trustee of the decedent's revocable trust, or the decedent's guardian.

The small estate affidavit

With this form, certain people collect the decedent's money and property without opening a court case, as long as the estate is $50,000 or less in gross value. Under Wis. Stat. 867.03(1g), the users can be an heir, the trustee of a revocable trust, a person named in the will as personal representative, or the decedent's guardian.

  • The affidavit must describe the property and its value, and state the total value of the estate.
  • A person named in the will who is not also an heir must wait 30 days before the holder of property transfers it under the affidavit.
  • If the decedent or the decedent's spouse ever received long-term care program services or medical assistance benefits, the affiant must first notify the Department of Health Services and attach proof of mail delivery.

The State Bar of Wisconsin maintains the form, and whoever signs it takes on legal responsibilities.

Register of deeds route for a house

A surviving spouse or beneficiary can end the decedent's interest in real property by filing an application with the register of deeds. Wis. Stat. 867.046(2) names who may apply: the spouse, a beneficiary of a marital property agreement, a transfer on death beneficiary, or a beneficiary of certain survivorship transfers.

  • The application for real property includes the latest property tax bill and a legal description.
  • For a joint tenancy, life estate or TOD designation, add a copy of the deed that created the interest.
  • Recording the application ends the decedent's interest, with the same force as a court-issued confirmation.
  • If the spouse or beneficiary does not start a confirmation proceeding within 90 days after death, any interested person may apply.

A good-faith buyer or lender who pays value takes title free of estate claims, with no duty to ask whether the transfer was proper.

Deadlines for personal representatives

When the court appoints the personal representative, it issues a Notice of Estate Administration Deadlines with the dates that apply. The main dates and duties:

  • The Inventory is due on the date shown in that notice, with a statutory filing fee.
  • The personal representative takes the notice to creditors to a newspaper for publication and mails a copy to each known creditor.
  • An objection, offset or counterclaim to a claim must be served and filed within 60 days after the claim was mailed or served.
  • The estate can close after the claims deadline runs out, and should close within 12 months of opening.
  • An extension needs a Petition for Extension of Time (PR-1833) and an order (PR-1834).
  • If no proceedings are pending six months after the Statement to Close Estate is filed, the appointment ends.

The estate also needs a Closing Certificate for Fiduciaries, which comes from filing Schedule CC with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.

Transfer fee and condition report when heirs sell

Two statutes touch an inherited home. Transfers by will, descent or survivorship are exempt from the real estate transfer fee under s. 77.25(11). Ask the register of deeds how the fee applies to the later sale to a buyer.

Under Wis. Stat. 709.01(2)(d), fiduciaries appointed or supervised by a court are excused from the condition report if they never occupied the property. An heir who lived in the house stands differently and should ask a Wisconsin attorney or the buyer's closing agent whether the report applies.

The Probate Registrar supplies certified copies of the Domiciliary Letters for a nominal statutory fee, so order enough for the title company and the buyer. Also ask the county treasurer for the current tax bill.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a lawyer for probate in Wisconsin?

Not for informal administration or summary settlement. Formal administration requires an attorney, and you must be represented in proceedings before a judge. Speak with one early if a claim may need to be disallowed.

How long does Wisconsin probate take?

An estate can close after the claims deadline runs out, and should close within 12 months of opening. The Probate Registrar can grant more time on a petition for extension.

Where do I file a Wisconsin probate case?

In the county where the decedent lived at death. If the decedent was not a Wisconsin resident, any county where Wisconsin property is located can take the application. Call that county's Register in Probate about appointments.

Can I sell the house before probate is finished?

Yes, once you hold court-issued letters as personal representative and sign a deed with the full legal description. Selling real estate is one of the personal representative's tasks. Spouses and certain beneficiaries may instead use the register of deeds route in Wis. Stat. 867.046.

What is the small estate limit in Wisconsin?

The limit is $50,000 in gross value. It applies to the transfer by affidavit under Wis. Stat. 867.03(1g) and to summary settlement and summary assignment.

Wisconsin tax on a home sale gain

There is no stand-alone capital gains tax here. Profit on a house is folded into ordinary Wisconsin income tax, with a 30 percent subtraction for net long-term gain. The Department of Revenue's Publication 103 notes that the capital gain in Wisconsin income can differ from the federal figure, because Wisconsin allows a deduction for 30 percent of the net capital gain from assets held more than one year.

So two layers apply. Federal rules, including the home sale exclusion, decide how much gain is taxable at all. Wisconsin then starts from your federal adjusted gross income and makes its own adjustments, such as the 30 percent subtraction.

How much of the gain Wisconsin taxes

If you held the house over a year, Wisconsin taxes 70 percent of what is left of the long-term gain after federal rules. The deduction is 30 percent of net capital gain from assets held more than a year, and 60 percent for farm assets held more than a year. Long-term means you owned the asset for more than one year; one year or less is short-term and gets no subtraction.

Whatever stays in Wisconsin taxable income is taxed at your marginal Wisconsin rate. A house owned for eleven months is short-term, so none of its gain gets the break.

The 60 percent rate is written for farm assets. A seller of an ordinary residence should plan on 30 percent. If you think the farm rate applies to you, read the Schedule WD instructions or ask the Department of Revenue.

Federal home sale exclusion

Up to $250,000 of gain on a main home is shielded federally, or $500,000 on a joint return. Because Wisconsin builds on federal adjusted gross income, excluded gain never shows up in the state calculation. IRS Topic 701 gives the tests.

  • Ownership: title for at least 24 months within the 5 years before closing.
  • Use: residence there for at least 24 months within those same 5 years, though not necessarily the same 24 months.
  • Joint filers: either spouse can satisfy ownership, but both need to satisfy use.
  • Another home's excluded gain within the prior two years generally blocks the exclusion.

If you receive a Form 1099-S, report the sale even when the entire gain is excludable. You also report it when part of the gain can't be excluded, and that remainder goes on federal Form 8949 and Schedule D. The exclusion covers a main home, so a rental or a house you never lived in has to be tested against the same two rules.

Wisconsin income tax rates

Wisconsin has four rates for 2025, from 3.5 percent to 7.65 percent, and a taxable gain is stacked on top of your other income. These brackets reflect 2025 Wisconsin Act 15.

RateSingle, head of householdMarried filing jointly
3.50%$0 to $14,679$0 to $19,579
4.40%$14,680 to $50,479$19,580 to $67,299
5.30%$50,480 to $323,289$67,300 to $431,059
7.65%$323,290 and up$431,060 and up

A large gain can push you into a higher bracket in the year of sale. The 70 percent left after the subtraction is the amount taxed at these rates. Brackets move with inflation and legislation, so use the table for the year you close.

Reporting the sale on a Wisconsin return

Individuals report the gain on Wisconsin Schedule WD, and the result flows to Schedule AD or Schedule SB of Form 1. An adjustment from Schedule WD goes on line 2 of Schedule AD, which is an addition, or line 5 of Schedule SB, which is a subtraction. The 30 percent deduction on a long-term gain lands on Schedule SB.

  • Residents file Form 1 with Schedule WD.
  • Form 1NPR is for nonresidents and part-year residents, who follow its instructions.
  • A mutual fund or REIT capital gain distribution alone doesn't need Schedule WD on Form 1, though Form 1NPR filers still complete it.

A house that closes in 2026 belongs on the 2026 return, so use that year's forms.

If the house sells at a loss

You can't deduct a loss on a home you lived in; personal-use property such as a house or car doesn't qualify. A loss on a rental house or other investment property can offset gains.

Wisconsin follows the same ceiling as federal law for capital losses. From tax year 2023, when losses exceed gains, you may deduct up to $3,000 of the excess against other income ($1,500 if married filing separately), and the rest carries forward with no time limit. A Wisconsin carryover can differ from the federal one, so the Schedule WD figure may not match your federal return.

Inherited houses

An inherited house's gain runs from the owner's basis; IRS Publication 551 explains basis for inherited or gifted property. Property from a decedent is also an exception to the normal long-term test, detailed in Publication 544.

One Wisconsin difference exists. Land acquired by inheritance and valued differently for Wisconsin inheritance tax and federal estate tax purposes can carry a different basis, but that applies only to deaths before January 1, 1992. A recent inheritance doesn't raise the issue.

Federal capital gains rates

Expect the federal bill to be bigger. For 2025 most net capital gain faces a rate of 15 percent at most, with these taxable income thresholds:

  • 0 percent rate: up to $48,350 for single filers and $96,700 for married filing jointly.
  • 15 percent rate: above those amounts up to $533,400 for single filers and $600,050 for married filing jointly.
  • 20 percent rate: above the 15 percent thresholds.

Short-term gain counts as ordinary income. A rental house that was depreciated can produce unrecaptured section 1250 gain, taxed at 25 percent at most. High earners may also owe the net investment income tax described in IRS Topic 559, and a large gain can require estimated tax payments (Topic 409).

Deferring the gain

Wisconsin offers a deferral federal law lacks, but it is for investing in a qualified Wisconsin business, not for buying another house. A taxpayer may defer tax on a long-term gain invested in a qualified Wisconsin business within 180 days, using Schedule CG, and the basis in the new investment drops by the deferred gain. Long-term gain on such an investment held at least five uninterrupted years can qualify for exclusion from Wisconsin income.

An installment sale works differently. Federal default reports gain as payments arrive, and a Wisconsin election can differ from the federal one. If you will carry a note for the buyer, plan the reporting with a tax professional before signing the contract. A cash sale avoids the question, since you receive the full price at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Does Wisconsin tax the profit when I sell my home?

Yes, as ordinary income, after a 30 percent subtraction for net long-term gain. The federal exclusion of up to $250,000 ($500,000 joint) can wipe out the gain before Wisconsin ever sees it.

What is the Wisconsin capital gains deduction?

A 30 percent subtraction applies to net gain on assets held over a year, rising to 60 percent for farm assets. Schedule WD does the math.

What are the Wisconsin income tax rates for 2025?

They are 3.5, 4.4, 5.3 and 7.65 percent. For a single filer the 5.3 percent bracket runs from $50,480 to $323,289, and 7.65 percent applies above $323,289.

Can I deduct a loss on a home I lived in?

No, a home you lived in produces no deductible loss. A rental or investment house can offset capital gains, and up to $3,000 of other income per year in Wisconsin.

Where do I report the sale on my Wisconsin return?

Use Schedule WD, which flows to line 2 of Schedule AD or line 5 of Schedule SB on Form 1. Nonresidents and part-year residents file Form 1NPR instead.

How a land contract sale works

With a Wisconsin land contract, the buyer pays the seller in installments and receives a deed once the contract is fully paid. The seller is called the vendor and the buyer the purchaser or vendee, the labels used in statutes and court decisions.

Put the deal on paper. Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(e) voids a contract to convey that lacks the signature of every party or their agent. A handshake deal or an unsigned payment ledger cannot carry a property transfer.

The vendor holds the deed, yet the vendee has real rights. In Steiner v. Wisconsin American Mutual Insurance Company, 2005 WI 72, the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that equitable title stays with the vendee until a circuit court enters an order confirming default after the redemption period ends.

When the buyer stops paying

A vendor cannot simply retake the house. The case goes to court, and the buyer gets at least 7 working days to redeem. Wis. Stat. 846.30 governs strict foreclosure of a land contract. If the court finds the buyer owes payments and has not made them, and the vendor is entitled to strict foreclosure, it sets a redemption period of at least 7 working days counted from the judgment hearing or, when there is no hearing, from entry of the judgment order.

No strict foreclosure judgment is final until the court enters an order, after the redemption period, confirming that nobody redeemed. Only then does the judgment become absolute.

The minimum period exists so a court cannot leave the buyer without a chance to redeem. A court of appeals decision also holds that every person holding the right can waive it by agreement.

Since the buyer's rights end only through that court order, a vendor tired of a stalled contract can call the circuit court clerk where the land sits and ask how to open a strict foreclosure case and what it costs to file.

Transfer fee on a land contract

The seller (grantor) owes the state's 30 cents per $100 of value or fraction, which is $3 per $1,000. On a land contract the measure is every dollar of principal the buyer promises to pay. Payment goes to the register of deeds along with the document being recorded, plus a transfer return that both sides sign (Wis. Stat. 77.22(1)).

SituationFee treatment

Transfer by will, descent or survivorshipExempt

Section 77.21(1) counts contracts and assignments of a vendee's interest as conveyances. If a buyer sells their position to someone else, ask the register of deeds how the fee treats that assignment.

Disclosures a land contract seller must give

A land contract seller of a home with one to four units owes the buyer a condition report. The disclosure statute, Wis. Stat. 709.01(1), reaches sales, exchanges and land contracts, except transfers that are exempt from the fee.

  • The report is due within 10 days after acceptance of the contract of sale or option contract.
  • A buyer who gets no report in that time may rescind in writing within 2 business days after the 10-day period ends and recover deposits.
  • A report counts as complete only when the owner answered or supplied information on every item.
  • Personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-supervised fiduciaries who never occupied the property are excused.

Condominium sellers add the association name, assessment amounts and a contact person to the report.

If the vendor or vendee dies

A deceased vendor's interest can move by application at the register of deeds instead of a court case. Under Wis. Stat. 867.046(2), the decedent's spouse, a beneficiary of a marital property agreement, a transfer on death beneficiary, or a beneficiary of certain survivorship transfers can apply to the register of deeds in the property's county.

  • For real property, the application includes a copy of the latest property tax bill and a legal description.
  • Once recorded, the application is prima facie evidence of the facts it recites and ends the decedent's interest.
  • If nobody starts a confirmation proceeding within 90 days after death, any interested person may apply.
  • A good-faith buyer or lender who pays value gets title clear of estate claims and need not investigate further.

Ask the register of deeds for the application form and whether the office takes it in person or by mail.

Property tax credits for land contract buyers

The lottery and gaming credit is open to a land contract buyer living in the home as a primary residence, provided the land contract, or an instrument evidencing it, is notarized no later than six months after the January 1 certification date.

The credit stays with a property sold after January 1 and should be counted when taxes are prorated between buyer and seller. Check the current bill with the county treasurer to see if the credit shows.

Annotations to s. 815.20 also say a land contract vendee has an interest sufficient to support the homestead exemption, which protects up to $75,000 against creditors.

Before you sell the home or the contract

Gather documents first, then choose: wait for the contract to run out, or sell the vendor's position. Any cash buyer will ask to see the signed contract, the payment record and any recorded memorandum.

  • Ask the register of deeds whether the contract or a notice of it is recorded, and whether the transfer fee return was filed.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the tax bill and any credit shown on it.
  • Read the contract for a clause limiting assignment or sale before promising anything to a new buyer.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether any taxes are past due on the parcel.

A Wisconsin real estate attorney can say whether strict foreclosure or a negotiated payoff fits your facts. If the buyer is current, the usual path is simpler: collect the final payment, deliver the deed, and let the recorded paperwork show the contract is complete. A cash purchase of the vendor's position can also end the arrangement quickly, as long as the contract allows it.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a buyer have to redeem after a land contract judgment in Wisconsin?

The court must set a redemption period of at least 7 working days. Wis. Stat. 846.30 counts it from the judgment hearing or, with no hearing, from entry of the judgment order. The judgment is not final until a later order confirms that no redemption happened.

Who pays the transfer fee on a land contract?

The grantor pays it. The rate is 30 cents per $100 of value, and for a land contract the value is the total principal the buyer agrees to pay the seller. The register of deeds collects it at recording.

Is a land contract sale exempt from the condition report?

No, unless the transfer is exempt from the transfer fee or the seller is an excused fiduciary who never lived there. Wis. Stat. 709.01(1) names land contracts among the covered transfers for one-to-four unit property.

Does the buyer own the house during a land contract?

The buyer holds equitable title. A 2005 Wisconsin Supreme Court decision holds that equitable title stays with the buyer until a court order confirms default after the redemption period ends.

Can heirs of a land contract vendor sell the property?

They can once their interest is confirmed. The register of deeds route under Wis. Stat. 867.046 lets qualifying beneficiaries record an application, and a good-faith purchaser from them takes free of estate claims.

Seller costs set by Wisconsin law

Three duties fall on a Wisconsin seller by statute: paying the transfer fee on the deed, covering recording for any paper the seller has to file, and giving the buyer a condition report. Commission, title charges and how the year's property tax is split work differently, because your contract and settlement statement control them.

Start by pricing the transfer fee. It is created by Wis. Stat. 77.22, falls on the grantor, and is paid at the register of deeds' counter when the deed is recorded. Recording the document is a separate flat $30. The rest is negotiable, so have the closing agent write out an estimate before you sign.

The Wisconsin transfer fee

The rate works out to 30 cents on every $100 of value. Any piece of $100 left over counts as a whole $100.

"Value" is a defined term. Under Wis. Stat. 77.21(3), a conveyance that isn't a gift is valued at everything actually paid or promised, liens on the property included. Gifts, deeds for token consideration and exchanges are valued at an estimated open-market price. Land contracts use the principal the buyer promises to pay.

Exemptions from the transfer fee

Only conveyances that match a category in Wis. Stat. 77.25 escape the fee, and the deed itself must name the exemption. Homeowners most often run into these:

  • An inheritance, whether by will, descent or survivorship.
  • Lender-side foreclosure outcomes, including a deed in lieu to a mortgage holder or a land contract seller.

  • A trustee handing title to a beneficiary without real consideration.
  • A deed that fixes or confirms an earlier recorded conveyance and carries little or no consideration.
  • A deed whose only job is to give or release security for a debt unrelated to a conveyance.
  • A taking by condemnation, or land worth $1,000 or less.

When a land contract was recorded with the proper fee already paid, the seller's later deed is exempt too. Under 77.256, no city, village, town or county may add its own fee to an exempt conveyance.

The transfer return

A transfer return goes to the Department of Revenue with the value, the fee and any exemption, signed by both grantor and grantee. The register of deeds holds the conveyance until the completed return and fee arrive. Wis. Stat. 77.255 carves out a narrow set of cases that need no return.

Filing happens online in My Tax Account, with no username or password, and a filer can also view or amend a return there. In a normal sale, your title company or attorney handles the filing. If you sign a deed on your own, the RETR page offers guides and the exemption list.

Collected fees are shared under Wis. Stat. 77.24, with 20 percent staying in the county and the balance going to the state. The department can revisit a return later, billing more fee or refunding an overpayment when the value was misreported or an exemption was claimed in error.

The real estate condition report

For one-to-four unit properties, the seller must deliver a filled-in condition report within 10 days after accepting an offer. The form, set out in Wis. Stat. 709.03, asks about structure, mechanical systems, environmental issues, wells, septic and storage tanks, taxes and special assessments, permits, and land use.

A late report lets the buyer walk away for two business days once the 10 days expire, with the deposit returned. A seller who learned something before acceptance that alters an answer must send an amended report or an amendment inside the same 10 days. Treat the form as a disclosure, not a warranty, and it won't stand in for inspections.

A few sellers are excused: a court-appointed fiduciary, such as a personal representative, who never occupied the property; an owner of a property that has never been inhabited; and any transfer exempt from the fee. The chapter covers sales, exchanges and land contracts.
